issues.legal_issue: A court may not decide a challenge that a gift was fraudulent or backdated when the challenge was not pleaded and the parties did not try the case on that issue.
material_facts: The written statement challenged the transfer and alleged collusion in bringing the suit, but did not allege that the gift was fraudulent or had been executed after the later sale.
No issue was framed on fraud or backdating, and no evidence was led with notice that either allegation would be decided.
The appellate court inferred backdating from a delay in registration and the non-production of a petition-writer’s register, although the respondents were not responsible for producing that register.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to set aside the findings of fraud and backdating because those matters had not been pleaded or tried, and the backdating finding lacked evidentiary support.
issues.legal_principle: A decision may address an unpleaded matter where the parties went to trial knowing it was in issue and adduced evidence on it, but not where the opposing party lacked notice and an opportunity to meet the case. The Court distinguished Kidar Lall Seal v. Hari Lall Seal, Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao, Kunju Kasavan v. M.M. Philip, and Union of India v. Khas Karanapura Colliery Ltd. It also held that a presumption could not be drawn against the respondents from the petition-writer’s failure to produce a register that they neither maintained nor possessed.

predicates.civil_property_title_suit: The proceeding was a civil suit seeking a determination of title to property.
predicates.challenged_transfer_was_not_pleaded_as_f: The party challenging the transfer did not plead that it was fraudulent or backdated.
predicates.parties_did_not_try_that_issue_with_noti: The parties did not proceed with notice that fraud or backdating was in issue or present evidence directed to that issue.

issues.definition: When a title suit includes an unpleaded challenge to a transfer that the parties did not try with notice and evidence, a finding on that challenge is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A gift of property already subject to a mortgage does not defraud the mortgagee when the gift leaves the mortgagee’s rights unaffected.
material_facts: The properties had already been mortgaged to the purchaser before the owner executed the gift.
The purchaser was shown to be the owner’s only creditor, and the loans were secured by the mortgages.
The donees could take the gifted properties only subject to the existing mortgages.
issues.conclusion: The gift could not defeat or delay the mortgagee’s rights, so the finding that it was fraudulent to defraud creditors was unjustified.
issues.legal_principle: A transfer subject to an existing mortgage does not impair the mortgagee’s rights under that mortgage. The Court relied on the facts that the mortgagee was the only creditor shown and that the loans were secured; it cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this point.

predicates.gift_transfer_challenged_as_creditor_fra: A party alleged that a gift was made to defraud or delay a creditor.
predicates.property_was_already_mortgaged_to_the_ch: The gifted property was already mortgaged to the creditor making the challenge.
predicates.donee_took_property_subject_to_mortgage: The donee acquired the property subject to the existing mortgage.

issues.definition: When a challenged gift transfers already mortgaged property subject to the mortgage, the gift does not defeat or delay the mortgagee’s rights.

issues.legal_issue: A party may not use an amendment on remand to introduce an entirely new, time-barred case of fraud or backdating.
material_facts: After the High Court remanded the case, the purchaser sought permission to amend the written statement to allege that the gift was fraudulent and backdated.
Those allegations were absent from the original written statement and would introduce a case different from the one originally pleaded.
The High Court had held that a suit on those pleas was already time-barred, and the Supreme Court considered it unfair to permit their introduction at that stage.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser could not amend the written statement to add the new pleas of fraud and backdating.
issues.legal_principle: The general rule disallows an amendment that sets up a new case or cause of action, particularly when a suit on that case would be barred by limitation. An amendment may nevertheless be allowed after limitation where it merely offers a different or additional approach to the same pleaded facts. The Court applied A.K. Gupta and Sons v. Damodar Valley Corporation and distinguished L.J. Leach and Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co.; the latter concerned a claim supported by allegations already in the pleading.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_remand_order: The proceeding was a civil appeal concerning an order remanding a case for further proceedings.
predicates.proposed_amendment_adds_a_new_case_not_b: The proposed amendment would introduce a distinct case rather than another approach to facts already pleaded.
predicates.new_case_is_time_barred: A suit based on the newly proposed case would be barred by limitation.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning a remand, an amendment introducing a distinct, time-barred case rather than developing pleaded facts is refused.

issues.legal_issue: Permission to amend pleadings on remand to address res judicata does not authorize unrelated new pleas or reopen findings on matters the remand court did not address.
material_facts: The High Court remanded the case to reconsider res judicata and allowed amendments setting out the particulars of that plea.
The High Court also permitted the trial court to consider other amendments, but the Supreme Court construed these as amendments consequential to the res judicata plea.
The High Court’s order set aside the lower courts’ findings on the points it had considered, not findings on other issues that had not been before it.
issues.conclusion: The remand did not permit unrelated amendments alleging fraud or backdating, and it did not set aside findings on issues the High Court had not considered.
issues.legal_principle: An order must be read in the context of the issues it addresses: permission to amend a particular plea and make consequential amendments does not permit the introduction of unrelated new pleas, and setting aside findings on considered points does not set aside unconsidered findings. The Court relied on its construction of the High Court’s remand order and cited no earlier case or statutory provision for this point.

predicates.civil_case_remanded_to_reconsider_res_ju: The case was remanded for reconsideration of a res judicata plea.
predicates.amendment_permission_is_for_res_judicata: The permission to amend concerns particulars of the res judicata plea and amendments consequential to it.
predicates.other_findings_were_not_considered_on_ap: The appellate court did not consider the other findings made below.

issues.definition: When a case is remanded to reconsider res judicata with permission for related amendments, the remand does not reopen unconsidered findings or permit unrelated amendments.

issues.legal_issue: A limitation challenge to title derived through an earlier donor need not be decided when the claim is independently supported by a valid gift from the original owner.
material_facts: The respondents claimed title to part of the property under gifts from an earlier owner, whose rights the purchaser argued had been lost after possession proceedings and the failure to bring a timely suit.
The respondents also claimed title to the same property under a gift from the original owner.
The High Court’s removal of the findings against that latter gift left it as an independent basis for the respondents’ title.
issues.conclusion: The limitation issue concerning the earlier donor’s rights was immaterial and did not need to be decided because the respondents’ title to the relevant property was supported by the gift from the original owner.
issues.legal_principle: Where a claimant’s title is independently established through another valid transfer, a challenge to an alternative chain of title need not be resolved. The Court referred to the earlier limitation argument under Article 47 of the Limitation Act, 1908, but did not decide its merits.

predicates.civil_property_title_suit: The proceeding was a civil suit seeking a determination of title to property.
predicates.claimant_has_an_independent_valid_title_: The claimant has a valid and independent basis for title to the property in dispute.
predicates.alternative_title_chain_is_not_needed_to: The challenged alternative chain of title is unnecessary to establish the claimant’s title.

issues.definition: When a claimant’s property title is independently supported and an alternative title chain is unnecessary, a limitation issue concerning that alternative chain is not decided.
